YAML vs JSON: syntax, types and conversion

YAML and JSON can describe the same supported values with different notation. The practical question is which types, conventions and parser behavior your configuration or data exchange needs.

By ParseCove · Published 27 November 2026

On this pageSame dataTry the typesType rulesWhat conversion losesChoose a formatFAQ

Start with one configuration in two formats

The example below describes a service, a boolean flag and an owner. The owner ID is text: its leading zeroes matter. Both representations can describe those values. YAML adds a comment and uses indentation for the nested mapping; JSON makes the object structure explicit with braces and commas.

YAML configuration

# Configuration for a local tool
service: ParseCove
enabled: true
owner:
  id: "001"
  name: Ada

The same supported data in JSON

{
  "service": "ParseCove",
  "enabled": true,
  "owner": {
    "id": "001",
    "name": "Ada"
  }
}

Formatting is not the data model. A newline, a comment or a different quote style can make a file easier to maintain without becoming a value that an application receives. Conversely, removing quotes from a value can change its type in some schemas. Before converting configuration, identify which values must stay strings, numbers, booleans, arrays or mappings.

Try the types

Choose a complete example. The output is generated by the same YAML 1.2 core parser and validation rules as the conversion tool.

{ "service": "ParseCove", "enabled": true, "owner": { "id": "001", "name": "Ada" } }

YAML 1.2 core: supported values are preserved.

The comment and presentation are discarded; supported data values remain.

Syntax is only part of the difference

This guide’s examples use the YAML 1.2 core schema and JSON values supported by the ParseCove converter. YAML processors can use other schemas, tags and version conventions. A result from a YAML 1.1 application is not automatically interchangeable with one from a 1.2 core parser.

ConcernYAML 1.2 core exampleJSON representation or decision
Booleanenabled: true{"enabled":true}
yes / noanswer: yes{"answer":"yes"} here; do not assume YAML 1.1 behavior
Identifierid: "001"Keep "001" as text
Date-looking textdate: 2026-11-27A string with this schema, not a JSON Date type
Missing-like valuemissing: nullnull, different from "" and an absent member
Sequenceitems: [red, blue]An array of two strings
Mapping key"1": firstJSON member names are strings; make that intent explicit

JSON has a compact set of value types; it does not define a native date, comment, alias or non-finite number. A parser may additionally restrict integer precision or duplicate members. ParseCove rejects duplicate keys and integers outside the JavaScript safe integer range in these tools, rather than silently selecting or rounding a value. That is a stated conversion policy, not a claim that every JSON processor behaves identically.

References: YAML 1.2.2 specification and RFC 8259: JSON values and interoperability.

What a data conversion can lose

Conversion keeps the supported values, not the original document. YAML comments, spacing, quote choices, block styles and source formatting do not survive as JSON values. Reverse conversion can create a readable YAML document, but cannot reconstruct comments that were discarded. Do not use a round trip as a source-file formatter if you need presentation preserved.

An alias such as secondary: *colors can refer to an earlier sequence. JSON can repeat the sequence’s values, but it has no anchor notation or shared-reference identity. A cyclic alias cannot become a finite JSON value tree. This tool also rejects excessive alias expansion, multiple documents, merge keys and unsupported tags; split or normalize those inputs deliberately before conversion.

Input featureWhat to verify
Comments and layoutRetain the original file if maintainers need its explanations
Duplicate keysChoose the intended value at the source; do not depend on an overwrite rule
AliasesCheck expansion, size and whether identity has meaning to the application
Large integer IDsQuote exact identifiers before passing through number-based tooling
Tags or application-specific typesDecide on an explicit JSON representation with the consuming application

A successful conversion checks the format and supported value model. It does not prove that a Kubernetes manifest, CI pipeline or application configuration satisfies its own schema. Validate the converted document with the consuming application as a separate step.

Choose the format around the workflow

For a file maintained by people, comments, readable nesting and familiar team conventions may favor YAML. The same flexibility also makes parser version, indentation and implicit type rules important review topics. For program-to-program exchange, JSON’s small value model and widespread parsers can make the contract easier to specify. Neither format automatically makes the contained data accurate or appropriate for an application.

Ask three concrete questions: Who edits this file? Which parser and schema reads it? Which values must retain their type and exact text? Keep the original document during migration, compare representative parsed values, and check the receiving application’s requirements before replacing configuration.

Use the YAML ↔ JSON converter to try your own supported document. Both .yaml and .yml file extensions are accepted; the extension alone does not establish a version or schema. For rectangular records, the CSV ↔ JSON tool makes a different set of choices about headers, strings and empty cells. If an API gives you a string containing JSON instead of an object, see the JSON encoding-layer guide.

Common questions

Is JSON valid YAML?

YAML 1.2 was designed for JSON compatibility, but the parser, schema, accepted constructs and interoperability policies still matter. Do not infer that every JSON implementation and every YAML configuration system accept or resolve all inputs the same way.

Is YAML always better for configuration?

No. Follow the consuming application’s supported format and your team’s editing workflow. Comments can help humans, while a narrow data contract can reduce interpretation choices. Validate the actual schema either way.

Why did a date or yes/no change type in another program?

A different YAML version, schema or explicit tag may resolve the scalar differently. These examples use 1.2 core, where yes stays text and untagged date-looking values stay strings. Quote exact text and document the parser assumptions.

Can conversion preserve comments?

A value conversion to ordinary JSON cannot store YAML comments as comments. Keep the original source or use a document-aware editing workflow when presentation matters.
